threads.topic: How long the internal borrowing lasts

entries.q: Internal borrowing is forecast at £92.7m at 31 March 2026 while usable reserves fall from £126.5m to £112.9m and investments from £50.2m to £35.8m. On the strategy's own forecast, in which year does the cash stop covering the borrowing need, and what borrowing rate is assumed at that point?
entries.why: The balance sheet forecast runs internal borrowing flat at roughly £92m to 2029 while reserves keep falling. The two lines converge; the strategy does not say when.

entries.q: 2025/26 delivered £34.2m of a £46.1m programme, with borrowing at £5.3m against £9.2m budgeted. The 2026/27 programme is £102.7m with £30.6m of borrowing. What changed in delivery capacity to support three times last year's actual spend?
entries.why: Underspend is not neutral. It moves MRP and interest into later years, and the £1.121m MRP saving reported at outturn is a one-off that reverses as the spend lands.

entries.q: The investment strategy commits to disposing of the £44.3m out-of-district portfolio after lease re-gearing, having confirmed a consistent fall in capital values at the 31 March 2026 valuation. If a disposal realises less than the outstanding debt attributable to the asset, how is the shortfall charged, and over what period?
entries.why: Capital receipts offset the CFR at the price achieved, not at book value. A portfolio bought with borrowing and sold below cost leaves MRP running on debt with no asset behind it.

entries.q: The 2026/27 programme commits £30.6m of new borrowing and the balance sheet carries £92.7m of internal borrowing against reserves that are falling. What is being handed to the successor authority under reorganisation, and has any of it been agreed with the other Nottinghamshire authorities?
entries.why: Reorganisation pools debt and reserves. Commitments made now are repaid by a body that did not approve them, and the £566k LGR reserve is the only line acknowledging it.

summary.text:
A district council carrying £175.4m of capital financing requirement against £82.7m of actual external borrowing. The £92.7m gap is funded from its own cash — the council's balance sheet forecast calls it internal borrowing — and that cash is running down: usable reserves fall from £126.5m to £112.9m across the year and treasury investments from £50.2m to £35.8m. Internal borrowing is only free while there is something to borrow from.

The 2026/27 capital programme is £102.7m (£58.4m HRA, £44.3m General Fund) with £30.6m of new borrowing attached. In 2025/26 the council set a £46.1m programme and delivered £34.2m of it — a £12.0m underspend, with borrowing coming in at £5.3m against £9.2m budgeted. The plan for next year is three times what was actually delivered last year.

The slippage is why MRP came in at £2.706m against a £3.827m budget, and why the CFR will probably land below the £175.4m the strategy forecast. It is a saving that repeats only once: the spend has moved, not gone.

Affordability is moving the wrong way. General Fund financing costs run at 11.60% of net revenue in 2025/26, 12.72% in 2026/27 and 12.93% in 2027/28; the HRA ratio falls slightly, from 7.76% to 7.46%. The out-of-district commercial property portfolio stands at £44.3m, fell 4.2% (£1.95m) in 2024/25, and the June 2026 investment strategy confirms 'a consistent downward movement in capital values across the majority' of it at the 31 March 2026 valuation. That strategy stops new out-of-district acquisitions and commits to disposal after lease re-gearing, with receipts to offset borrowing or be reinvested locally. At outturn the property investments line was £568k over budget.

Two things sit behind all of it. The council repaid its Dexia loan and two PWLB loans in 2025/26, which is why net interest came in £172k under budget — a smaller book, but the LOBO exposure in the maturity chart has not gone. And Ashfield is a Nottinghamshire district inside local government reorganisation: a £566k LGR reserve was created in 2025/26 and £1m of the General Fund surplus transferred into it. The £102.7m programme and the £30.6m of borrowing behind it will be delivered, and repaid, by a successor authority.
